nameStory: The Northern Lapwing gets its name from its distinctive flight pattern — it appears to 'lap' through the air with slow, irregular wingbeats that look almost lazy or floppy. The alternative name 'peewit' comes from its sharp, piercing call that sounds exactly like 'pee-wit' or 'pee-wee-wit' echoing across open fields.
description: The Northern Lapwing is a striking medium-sized shorebird about the size of a robin, but chunkier and longer-legged. It sports a dramatic wispy black crest that curves backward from its head, giving it a punk-rock appearance. Its back shimmers with an iridescent green and purple sheen, while its belly is bright white with a bold black breast band that's especially prominent in breeding males.

idTips.label: Wispy Black Crest
idTips.description: A thin, curved black feather plume extends backward from the head, often bouncing as the bird walks — no other plover in New England has this distinctive punk-rock hairdo

idTips.label: Iridescent Back
idTips.description: The back and wings shimmer with metallic green and purple hues that shift and gleam in sunlight, feeling almost oil-slick smooth if you could touch it

idTips.label: Floppy Flight Style
idTips.description: Flies with slow, irregular wingbeats that look almost butterfly-like — the broad, rounded wings seem to 'lap' through the air rather than beat steadily

idTips.label: Sharp 'Pee-wit' Call
idTips.description: Gives a piercing, nasal 'pee-wit' or 'pee-wee-wit' call that carries far across open areas — sounds almost like a squeaky gate or bicycle brake

idTips.label: Bold Black Breast Band
idTips.description: A thick black stripe across the white chest that's especially prominent in breeding males, creating a sharp contrast like a formal vest

habitat: Northern Lapwings are extremely rare visitors to New England, typically appearing in short-grass fields, golf courses, airports, and muddy farm fields during migration. When they do show up, look for them in open areas with sparse vegetation where they can spot predators easily, often mixing with other plovers or shorebirds near temporary puddles or wet spots.

seasonality.spring: Rare vagrant birds might appear in March through May, usually after strong storm systems blow them off their normal migration routes. Look for tired-looking individuals in farm fields or coastal areas.
seasonality.summer: Extremely unlikely to be seen, as this species breeds in Europe and Asia. Any summer sighting would be extraordinary and require careful documentation.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring, with most records occurring in September through November. Birds may appear disheveled after long ocean crossings.
seasonality.winter: Very rare but possible, especially during mild winters. Any wintering bird would likely frequent reliable food sources like golf courses or unfrozen agricultural areas.

funFact: Northern Lapwings are master actors — when predators approach their ground nest, parent birds will fake a broken wing, dragging it dramatically while crying pitifully to lure threats away from their chicks, then suddenly 'recover' and fly off once the danger has been led far enough away.
confusionNotes: The wispy black crest makes lapwings unmistakable among New England birds — no other plover or shorebird has this feature. The closest confusion might be with Killdeer, but Killdeer have two black breast bands (not one) and lack the crest entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Northern' Lapwing, this species is actually from Europe and Asia — the 'Northern' refers to its range within the Old World, not North America. Every sighting in New England represents a remarkable vagrant that has crossed the Atlantic Ocean, making each observation precious for birders.
compareHints: As the only lapwing species recorded in New England, compare it to other plovers in the family. Unlike the smaller, brown-backed Killdeer with its double breast bands, or the compact Piping Plover with its pale sandy coloring, the Northern Lapwing is larger, darker above with that metallic sheen, and sports the unmistakable wispy black crest that no other regional plover possesses.
